title: The Future Is Domain-Specific Agents - Justin Schroeder, StandardAgents

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central thesis is composition over inheritance for structuring multi-agent systems as isolated domain-specific sub-agents coordinated by a parent agent, which is fundamentally about agent loops, multi-agent patterns, and harness architecture. The architectural patterns are domain-agnostic and aimed at software builders constructing agent systems. The talk focuses on architectural design principles and development patterns for agents, with secondary attention to production deployment challenges. The talk assumes familiarity with agents, MCP, and LLM systems but remains accessible to practitioners without deep ML expertise. Conference presentation delivered at the AI Engineer channel event. Claims derive from the speaker's experience at StandardAgents with self-reported quantitative metrics, not peer-reviewed research.

domains.rationale: The talk's central thesis is composition over inheritance for structuring multi-agent systems as isolated domain-specific sub-agents coordinated by a parent agent, which is fundamentally about agent loops, multi-agent patterns, and harness architecture. The architectural patterns are domain-agnostic and aimed at software builders constructing agent systems. The talk focuses on architectural design principles and development patterns for agents, with secondary attention to production deployment challenges. summary: Justin Schroeder, co-founder of StandardAgents, presents the case for domain-specific agents as the key architectural unlock for useful AI. He draws a parallel between the Industrial Revolution—harnessing energy with machines—and the current era—harnessing intelligence with agents. He defines agents as deterministic software harnessing non-deterministic model outputs toward desired objectives. Despite widespread agent development across organizations of all sizes, most people cannot name agents beyond Claude or Codex. The motivation is integration of business data with AI. Building robust agents is extremely difficult due to orchestration complexity, provider abstractions, durable execution, observability, portability, and composability failures. Organizations retreat to MCP and skills, but these inflate context through inheritance—adding attributes to expand capabilities. Skills degrade performance when overused, and inheritance breaks down at scale: 100 or 1,000 skills produce diminishing returns. The alternative is composition. Instead of one agent with all capabilities, build small, isolated domain-specific agents—each a full agent with its own system prompt, tools, message history, agentic loop, sandboxed file system, and sandboxed code execution. A coordinator agent communicates with these sub-agents in plain English. Schroeder draws an analogy to Apollo 11, where teams of specialized experts each had specific tools and capabilities. Sub-agents can be recursive: a coordinator might call a Salesforce agent, which itself calls an asset-generation sub-agent; a legal team agent might have GDPR and OSHA compliance sub-agents. Each agent maintains minimal context windows throughout the hierarchy, keeping the system highly efficient. StandardAgents reports over 80% token efficiency per task. Domain-specific agents enable small language models: DeepSeek V4 Flash is 137 times cheaper than Fable per task. They enforce strict capability limits, easing IT security concerns, and have excellent scaling characteristics as independent execution environments. However, domain-specific agents don't yet exist publicly. Schroeder predicts rapid adoption by end of 2026, with 2027 as the year of multi-agent orchestration, driven by rising token costs—up 29% adjusted for IQ and 76% in raw terms. The ideal agent architecture includes a tool layer of functions, prompts, and full agents as tools, hooks for side effects, agent rules for turn-taking governance, a sandboxed file system, and sandboxed code execution.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Composition over inheritance is the core architectural principle: build small isolated domain-specific agents instead of inflating one agent's context with more skills and tools.
Each domain-specific agent is a full agent with its own system prompt, tools, message history, agentic loop, sandboxed file system, and sandboxed code execution.

A coordinator agent communicates with sub-agents in plain English; sub-agents can be recursive, with specialized agents (Salesforce, legal, GDPR, OSHA) maintaining minimal context windows throughout the hierarchy.
Domain-specific agents achieve over 80% token efficiency per task by carrying only minimal, domain-relevant context.
Small language models become practical: DeepSeek V4 Flash is 137x cheaper than Fable per task when scoped to specific domains.
Domain-specific agents enforce strict capability limits—only explicitly approved actions—easing IT security and permissions concerns.
Token costs are rising in 2026: up 29% adjusted for IQ, up 76% in raw tokens, making efficiency critical for customer-facing AI.
Schroeder predicts rapid framework adoption by end of 2026 and declares 2027 the year of multi-agent orchestration.
Every agent should have its own sandboxed file system and sandboxed code execution location as baked-in primitives, enabling safe file writing and execution without OS-level risks.

sections.title: Introduction and Industrial Revolution Analogy
sections.summary: Schroeder introduces himself and StandardAgents, draws a parallel between the Industrial Revolution (harnessing energy with machines) and the current era (harnessing intelligence with agents), and defines agents as deterministic software harnessing non-deterministic model outputs.

sections.title: Everyone Is Building Custom Agents—But Why?
sections.summary: Despite few people being able to name agents beyond Claude or Codex, organizations of all sizes are building custom agents. The core motivation is integration—businesses want their data properly integrated with AI for competitive gains.

sections.title: Why Building Robust Agents Is Hard
sections.summary: Building custom agents is extremely difficult due to agentic loop orchestration, provider abstractions, durable execution, validations, telemetry and observability at scale, portability failures, and lack of composability. Agents work as demos but fail in production.

sections.title: MCP and Skills as Incomplete Solutions
sections.summary: Organizations retreat to MCP, which works as a de facto tool distribution mechanism but only meaningfully supports tools. Skills are markdown documentation that help but degrade agent performance when overused. Neither tools nor documentation alone solve the fundamental problem.

sections.title: The Agent Stack and the Inheritance Problem
sections.summary: Schroeder constructs the agent stack: model, system prompt, tools, skills, MCP, and messages—nearly all context. Integration efforts inflate context or improve models, equating to inheritance. Inheritance works but is not the fundamental solution.

sections.title: Composition Over Inheritance: Domain-Specific Agents
sections.summary: The alternative to inheritance is composition. Instead of one agent loaded with all capabilities, build small isolated domain-specific agents—each a full agent with its own system prompt, tools, message history, and agentic loop. A coordinator agent communicates with sub-agents in plain English. Schroeder draws an analogy to Apollo 11 teams of specialized experts as a form of biomimicry.

sections.title: Benefits of Domain-Specific Agents
sections.summary: Domain-specific agents are far more token efficient (over 80%), practical with small language models (DeepSeek V4 Flash is 137x cheaper than Fable per task), enforce strict capability limits for better security, and have excellent scaling characteristics as independent execution environments. However, they don't yet exist publicly.

sections.title: Predictions and Rising Token Costs
sections.summary: Schroeder predicts rapid adoption of domain-specific agents by end of 2026 and declares 2027 the year of multi-agent orchestration. Token costs are rising: up 29% adjusted for IQ and 76% in raw tokens in 2026. Customer-facing AI needs efficiency since large models are too expensive to put in front of customers without massive lifetime value.

sections.title: Ideal Agent Architecture: Tools, Hooks, and Rules
sections.summary: Schroeder outlines an ideal agent architecture. The tool layer includes functions (executable code), prompts (sub-prompts that call other LLMs or image generators), and full-blown domain-specific agents as tools. Hooks can mutate state or perform side effects, such as injecting current time as an artificial message. Agent rules govern turn-taking and execution constraints.

sections.title: File Systems, Sandboxed Execution, and Recursive Sub-Agents
sections.summary: Schroeder elaborates on agent rules (turn limits, tool validation), then adds two essential primitives: every agent should have its own sandboxed file system and sandboxed code execution location, enabling safe file writing and execution without OS-level risks. He demonstrates recursive sub-agent architecture with concrete examples: a coordinator agent calling a Salesforce agent (which calls an asset-generation sub-agent with image and SVG tools), a Google Workspace agent for spreadsheets, a legal team agent with separate GDPR and OSHA compliance sub-agents. Each agent maintains minimal context windows throughout the hierarchy. He closes by inviting businesses to sign up for early access at standardagents.ai.

limitations: Domain-specific agents do not yet exist publicly in a significant way.
Inheritance breaks down at scale: 100 or 1,000 skills produce diminishing returns.
Agents are not portable—work on one machine but frequently fail on another.
Agents are not composable—cannot easily reuse a working agent across different use cases.
MCP only meaningfully supports tools; other capabilities remain sparse.
Excessive use of skills makes agents substantially worse per cited research.
Telemetry and observability on agents is very hard, especially at scale.
Domain-specific agents require more upfront task definition compared to general-purpose agents.
Small models like DeepSeek V4 Flash fail repeatedly at complex tasks, reducing cost advantage if used broadly.
quantitativeClaims: Domain-specific agents regularly achieve over 80% token efficiency for any given task.
DeepSeek V4 Flash is 137 times cheaper than Fable per task.
Token costs adjusted for IQ are up 29% in 2026.
Raw token costs are up 76% in 2026, nearly a 100% increase.
